title: Article Archive: Education The Questioning Traps: When Routines Lose Their Purpose
author: WAGOLL Teaching
summary: Strong questioning routines — turn and talk, cold calling, mini-whiteboards, think-pair-share — can drift from purposeful instructional tools into habit-driven time-fillers when their intent fades. WAGOLL Teaching identifies five specific traps: the 'Guess What's in the Teacher's Head' trap (asking about knowledge students don't yet have, producing active guessing not active learning); the First Letter Prompt trap (a clue that turns understanding into a word puzzle); the Turn and Talk Without Purpose trap (vague prompts that generate superficial conversation); the No Think Time trap (questions followed immediately by answers, creating cognitive overload and shallow participation); and the Vague Question trap (open-ended prompts that tell the teacher nothing about what students actually understand). Each trap is analyzed against research from Willingham, Rosenshine, Rowe, and Wiliam, and each is followed by a concrete corrective move rooted in the same principle: questions must direct pupils to think about the right knowledge, not search for words in the dark.
points: Questioning routines only work when they are driven by clear instructional intent — the routine is the vehicle, but the knowledge-linked prompt is the engine.

The 'Guess What's in the Teacher's Head' trap conflates active participation with active learning: students contributing guesses about knowledge they haven't yet been taught are performing retrieval on nothing, not building understanding.
The First Letter Prompt is a surface-level scaffold that supports word retrieval rather than conceptual thinking — a better prompt stays connected to meaning, not to the shape of the answer.

Wait time of even a few seconds before accepting responses leads to longer, more thoughtful answers and greater participation across the class — Rowe's research shows that removing the pressure to respond instantly changes who can contribute.

The best questions have a job to do: they reveal whether students have understood a specific idea, can explain key vocabulary, can apply a method, or can connect knowledge to an example — not whether they can fill silence.
quotes: As Daniel Willingham reminds us, 'memory is the residue of thought.' If our questions are not directing pupils to think about the right knowledge, then the routine itself is not doing the job we think it is.

This is not active learning. It is active guessing. If pupils do not have the knowledge, they cannot reason their way to the answer. They can only try to work out what is in the teacher's head. In these moments, the most helpful thing a teacher can do is often the most direct thing. Teach the knowledge first.

Giving pupils the first letter of a word is a good example. It feels like a scaffold, but it does not support understanding. Instead, it turns the task into a word puzzle and does not build scientific knowledge.
Without a precise prompt, it can quickly drift into low-level conversation or passive participation. Pupils may speak, but they are not necessarily thinking about the learning.

Research by Mary Budd Rowe showed that even a small increase in wait time leads to longer, more thoughtful responses and greater participation across the class. Giving pupils a few seconds to think allows more of them to process the question and formulate an answer.

As Dylan Wiliam argues, the quality of questioning is central to effective formative assessment. Precision matters because it allows teachers to see which parts of the lesson pupils understand, which components need reteaching, and where pupils are ready to think more deeply.
